messages.subject: French study in Auvergne
parts:
Hello,
 

For a study of 157 points transects on 2 years (2016 and 2017), we have used DS software with  3 key-functions and for each, two adjustements (cosine and simple polynomial) ; which represents 6 combinations. According to the species, we have used right and/or left truncature. Each time, we have selected the lowest AIC. We have tested first 2016, then 2017 and to finish 2016+2017.

We have today 3 questions about our results (see file attached) :

1)    BLACKCAP (page 3)

Between the results of the models M6 and M7, should we choose the chi2 value rather than the KS and CvM values ?

 

2)    CHAFFINCH (page 5)

The first results have given an irregular chart. We have grouped data into larger distance  bands ; the results are better. Do you recommend this option in this case?

 

3)    YELLOW-HAMMER (page 6 )

The data shows that contacts close to the observer are very numerous and no key-functions have given good result. How to do with this bias ?

Thanks in advance.

Best regards,

Gilles S.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] French study in Auvergne
parts:
Giles

A few general comments, then to your specific questions:

- Left-truncation of distance sampling data is troublesome; it is the shape of the detection function at very small distances that are central to estimating the fundamental parameters in distance sampling (f(0) for lines, h(0) for points). 

- The tables you provide are a good summary of the analyses you performed; the delta-AIC values would have made a useful contribution to the tables, but for the most part that can be deduced by the information you provided.

- To assess fit for point transect data, the probability density function graphs, rather than the detection probability graphs you provided may be more useful.

Your specific questions:

- blackcap: goodness of fit tests (chisquare, KS, CvM tests) are not really used for model selection.  The strategy is to apply models and determine whether they fit--i.e. produce p-values larger than 0.05.  All the models in your blackcap table meet this criterion.  The next step is then to examine delta-AIC scores to select the model most applicable.  In this case, M6 and M7 have different truncation - hence different data; and delta-AIC cannot be used to compare them.  You then use other assessments, visual assessment of agreement between data and probability density function to make your assessment.  In the end, you will note there is little difference in the 95% confidence interval estimates for M6 and M7, so it may be a distinction without a difference.

- chaffinch: note the trivial difference in the CI bounds for S4 and S4-2.  Both treatments of the data produce models that fit the data, and very similar estimates.

- yellowhammer: I don't know what model you have shown in the figure on page 6, but that figure suggests the fitted model is not trying to fit the surplus of detections at small distances.  The question to ask is what causes the large number of detections at those small distances.  This is less a statistical modelling issue than the reason for that rapid drop in numbers of detections at roughly 35m.  I suspect had you shown estimates from hazard rate models they would have produced much larger estimates than the uniform/half-normal key functions.
